row.short_label: MBCR 1:331 gunpowder-fine remission (2 June 1641)
row.statement: The Massachusetts General Court order of 2 June 1641 remitted the fine of John Porter, James Ludden, and John Gurney, incurred "for want of gunpowder."

row.short_label: MA Archives gunpowder petition (30 May 1641, 'of Weymouth')
row.statement: The underlying petition, calendared in the Massachusetts State Archives colonial collection and dated 30 May 1641, names "John Gurny, Richard Porter, and James Ludden of Weymouth" seeking remission of the gunpowder fines.

row.short_label: Porter (1878) gloss: 'Ludden and Gurney were of Weymouth'
row.statement: Porter's Genealogy of the Descendants of Richard Porter (1878), p. 225, quotes the 1641 court order and glosses it "Ludden and Gurney were of Weymouth."

row.short_label: Nash (1885): John an original Weymouth grantee before 1643
row.statement: Nash's Historical Sketch of Weymouth (1885), Appendix C, records East Field (p. 258) and Mill Field (p. 278) parcels "first granted to John Gurny/Gurnie" but already held by other men by the 1643 partial property record.

row.short_label: Earliest firm presence: Weymouth by 30 May/2 June 1641
row.statement: John Gurney was living at Weymouth, Massachusetts, by 30 May / 2 June 1641 — his earliest firm New England presence.

row.short_label: Arrival window: 1638–early 1641
row.statement: John Gurney reached New England in 1638–early 1641: bounded below by his original (pre-1643) Weymouth grants and his 1641 presence, and above by the sharp post-1640 falloff of the Great Migration.

row.short_label: Porter forename: petition 'Richard … of Weymouth' vs printed 'John'
row.statement: The petition's image-verified "Richard Porter of Weymouth" reading shifts weight from the printed order's "John Porter," making John Gurney's cleanest 1641 associate a Weymouth/Hull-company comparator rather than a Hingham/Salem Porter.

row.short_label: Braintree residence, c. 1645–1662/3
row.statement: John Gurney lived at Braintree, Massachusetts, from about 1645 until his death in 1662/3 — his settled colonial home after leaving Weymouth.

row.short_label: 1645 Braintree plantation petition (signed)
row.statement: In May 1645 John Gurney signed the inhabitants' petition for the new plantation at Braintree (Mount Wollaston), as reported in the History of Weymouth.

row.short_label: 1652/3 deposition: 'John Gurney of Brayntree'
row.statement: A Suffolk Court Files deposition of 17 March 1652/3 (Wilson v. Faxon) describes "John Gurney of Brayntree aged 50 Yeares or thereabouts."

row.short_label: Tyng farm lease, 1647–1662 (continuous tenancy)
row.statement: In 1647 William Tyng leased John Gurney a 45-acre Braintree farm for ten years; John continued to lease it from Tyng's daughters Bethia and Mercy until 1662, and the same farm is recorded in the 1653 Tyng inventory and the 28 March 1661 estate-division indenture.

row.short_label: Principal Braintree land was the leased Tyng farm (future Adams seat)
row.statement: John Gurney's principal Braintree landholding was leasehold, not freehold: the Tyng farm he held continuously c. 1647–1662 was a tenancy, and the northern part of 'the Gurney farm' later became the Adams family seat (the Old House, Quincy).

row.short_label: 1661/2 Gurney–Thayer deed ('John Gurney, tailor')
row.statement: On 12 February 1661/2 "John Gurney, tailor" conveyed to Richard Thayer, for £14, a Braintree house and orchard, a five-acre Monatiquot-River parcel, and an adjoining half-acre; possession given 16 April 1662, signed by mark, witnessed by Peter Brackett and John Rockwell.

row.short_label: Two distinct Braintree properties: leased Tyng farm vs. Monatiquot freehold
row.statement: John held two distinct Braintree properties in his final years — the leased Tyng farm (the future Adams seat) and his own Monatiquot-River freehold sold to Thayer in 1661/2 — so the 'Gurney farm' of local tradition and his personal homestead are separate parcels.

row.short_label: 1659 Baxter estate: witness and inventory-taker
row.statement: John Gurney witnessed Gregory Baxter's Braintree will in 1659 (with Moses Payne and Richard Brackett) and helped take the estate inventory on 7 July 1659.

row.short_label: Recognised standing in the Braintree community
row.statement: John Gurney held recognised standing in the Braintree community — signing the 1645 plantation petition, serving as probate witness and inventory-taker for Gregory Baxter (1659), and appearing across a dense Braintree creditor network in his own 1663 estate accounts.

row.short_label: Open: pin the 1645 Braintree petition to its primary source
row.statement: Locate the primary page of the May 1645 Braintree (Mount Wollaston) plantation petition naming John Gurney; the current basis is the secondary History of Weymouth report (research lead L-191).

row.short_label: Admitted Weymouth inhabitant (c. 1638/9-1642/4)
row.statement: John Gurney was an admitted, resident inhabitant of Weymouth c. 1638/9-c. 1642/4: early-Massachusetts town land divisions went only to admitted inhabitants, so his three original East/Mill-Field grants mark him as a recognised member of the Weymouth community before his removal to Braintree.

row.short_label: Manuscript Land Grants book: John original grantee of 3 parcels
row.statement: The Weymouth proprietors' manuscript Land Grants book records John Gurney as original grantee of three parcels - two East Field lots (ms pp. 12, 23, under Robert Randoll and Nathaniel Addames) and one Mill Field lot (ms p. 31, under Thomas Richardes), about eight acres in all - each 'first granted/given to John Gurny/Gurnie.'

row.short_label: MBCR 2:79 - 1644 £5 'Mr Ginner' bill (Gurny + Lake)
row.statement: The Massachusetts Bay colony accounts for the General Court session beginning 30 October 1644 record: 'John Gurny his byl for 3. 16. 4d & Tho: Lake his note for 1. 3. 8d are accepted for £5 fro Mr Ginner.'

row.short_label: Credit tie to Rev. Thomas Jenner, Weymouth's minister
row.statement: John Gurney held a credit tie to Rev. Thomas Jenner ('Mr Ginner'), Weymouth's minister 1636-1640: the 1644 colony accounts accepted his bill and Thomas Lake's note as the £5 Jenner owed. The purpose of Gurney's bill is unstated - not evidence of tailoring, military supply, or a 1641/2 transaction.

row.short_label: Weymouth associates: Ludden, Porter, Goodman King
row.statement: John Gurney's documented Weymouth associates were fellow townsmen - his 1641 gunpowder-fine co-petitioners James Ludden and Richard Porter (Porter a 1635 Weymouth settler) and, persisting to his 1663 estate, the creditor 'Goodman King of Waymouth.'

row.short_label: Negative: no active military service
row.statement: No record places John Gurney in active military service: the 1641 powder fine reflects only the ordinary readiness obligation, and a Gurn-variant sweep of the colony military/court records plus a full read of the printed colony records and the Military Company roll (1637-1652) finds him on no campaign, officer, volunteer, or membership list.

row.short_label: Billerica town book - 1659 grant-on-condition & surrender
row.statement: The Billerica manuscript town book records a ten-acre house-lot granted to John Gurney 15 August 1659 'upon condition' he inhabit it himself (his son Richard accepted as a fellow inhabitant), and on 26 December 1659 its surrender: 'Daniel Shead in answer for his father John Gurney; the said John Gurney surrendred up the Lott.'

row.short_label: Hazen Billerica - Dudley-Farm rate & absentee upland share
row.statement: Hazen's History of Billerica records John Gurney assessed 2 pounds 5s 10d toward the half-payment for the Dudley Farm purchase on 10 September 1659, and in the November 1659 upland division 'Peter Bracket and Joseph Tompson holding in common the right of John Gurney, of Braintree' - an absentee share held by other men.

row.short_label: Ballou - John among Braintree men allotted at Mendon, 1662
row.statement: Adin Ballou's History of Milford places John Gurney among the Braintree men accepted to allotments at the new Mendon (Nipmug) plantation in 1662.

row.short_label: SPR #338 - the 1663 'Quinapaug wch we know not' estate line
row.statement: John Gurney's 1663 Braintree probate inventory (taken 16 March 1663; total 55 pounds 14s 6d) records a land-interest line reading 'an estate layd out in land at Quinapaug wch we know not' - an interest the appraisers could not value.

row.short_label: Suffolk Deeds IV - Quinapaug (Providence-jurisdiction) tract, no Gurney in the recorded deeds
row.statement: Suffolk Deeds Liber IV records the Quinapaug tract: Joshua Foote bought 4,000 acres 'att Quinapaug within ye Jurisdiction of Providence' from the Indians Sacont and George Sacount by deed of 18 June 1655; by 1660 it passed to William Hudson, who sold it in 500-acre parcels to Boston men. No Gurney appears among the recorded Quinapaug parcels.

row.short_label: Finding: Billerica proprietorship (house-lot surrendered; Dudley-Farm share + meadow lots persist); never removed there
row.statement: John Gurney was admitted a proprietor of the new town of Billerica in 1659 - a standing carrying a personal ten-acre house-lot (granted 15 August 1659 on condition he inhabit it, his son Richard accepted as fellow inhabitant), a rate-paying share in the communal Dudley Farm purchase, and two great-meadow lots. He surrendered the house-lot within four months, handed back through his son-in-law Daniel Shed, and never removed to Billerica; the meadow and upland allocations appear in the records independently of the surrendered house-lot, but no Billerica parcel is shown passing to or occupied by a Gurney.

row.short_label: Finding: Quinapaug line = unrecorded Providence-jurisdiction frontier share
row.statement: The 1663 inventory's 'estate layd out in land at Quinapaug wch we know not' is best read as an unrecorded right or share in the Providence-jurisdiction Quinapaug land speculation (Foote to Hudson to Boston men) - an unvalued frontier proprietary interest, not appraised Braintree real estate.

row.short_label: Analysis: proprietary right, not residence (the 1659-1663 frontier pattern)
row.statement: In 1659-1663 John Gurney repeatedly took up proprietary rights in newly-forming plantations - a Billerica house-lot and Dudley-Farm proprietor's share (1659), a Mendon allotment (1662), and an unlocated Quinapaug frontier interest (by 1663) - and relocated to none of them; the same pattern includes the 1651/2 Weymouth Second-Division great lot granted after he had left that town. The record distinguishes taking up a proprietary right in a new plantation from removing there to live: John's home stayed in the established Weymouth-then-Braintree corridor (his own Monatiquot freehold with house and orchard, sold 1661/2, and the leased Tyng farm he held as tenant). This is proprietary right held separately from residence, not an absence of settlement - John was himself a settler and landholder across several new towns.

row.short_label: Open: Mendon post-1667 record vs John's 1662/3 death (right carried forward vs retrospective)
row.statement: Because Mendon was incorporated only 15 May 1667 and John died 1662/3, his name in the printed Mendon proprietors' record stream postdates his death: it is most plausibly an early 1662 grant carried forward into the later proprietor list or a retrospective allottee entry rather than proof of residence. Whether the 1662 acceptance and the post-incorporation lot are the same right - and how 'John Gurny' and 'Grisel Gurney' as twenty-acre lot-holders relate to the widow/descendants - is developed in the family-Mendon-descendants topic; the manuscript proprietors' images remain the pull.

row.short_label: 1663 probate inventory: itemized movable estate (£55 14s 6d)
row.statement: The manuscript inventory of John Gurney Senr's goods and estate, Braintree, 16 March 1663 (taken by Gregory Belcher, Edmund Quincy, and Thomas Faxon), itemizes his movable estate line by line — apparel, boots and hat; bedding, blanket, pillows and cases; pewter, pincers, brass skillet and kettle; a cupboard and a musket; plough-irons, coulter, axes, mattock and chisel; a chair and frame goods, barrels and trays; wheat and Indian corn with grain-boxes, hoops and tubs; a horse and yoke of oxen; sows, pigs and young cattle; an old barrow, wheels and axletree; and one unvalued land line 'an estate layd out in land at Quinapaug wch we know not' — appraised in all at £55 14s 6d.

row.short_label: Finding: estate wealth concentrated in livestock and the working farm
row.statement: John Gurney's working wealth at death was in husbandry, not his named tailoring trade: livestock alone (horse £9 10s + yoke of oxen £12 10s + swine £6 + young cattle £6) accounted for about £34 of the £55 14s 6d estate, and with plough-gear, cart equipment, and stored wheat and Indian corn the farm economy comes to roughly three-quarters of the whole appraisal.

row.short_label: Finding: a sparse but sufficient household
row.statement: John Gurney's household goods were modest and few — his own apparel, boots and hat (£4 5s) his single most valuable possession, plus bedding (£2 12s), a little pewter and brass (14s 6d), one cupboard (8s), a chair and frame goods, barrels and trays (16s 6d), and an ordinary household musket (12s), with no plate, glass, books, or surplus furniture — a working colonial home furnished to sufficiency and no further.

row.short_label: Negative: no tailoring tools or cloth in the estate
row.statement: The 1663 estate inventory contains no tool or stock of the tailoring trade — no shears, needles, thimble, pressing- or goose-iron, yard-measure, or cloth/fabric — despite John being styled 'John Gurney, tailor' in his 1661/2 Monatiquot conveyance. The absence does not unsay the trade (the deed is direct evidence) but qualifies its centrality to his late-life economy, whose appraised value sat in land-rights and livestock; the 'pincers' listed beside the pewter are a general household/smith's tool, not a tailor's implement.

row.short_label: Analysis: an all-movable estate with no valued real estate
row.statement: The 1663 appraisal is essentially all personalty because John held no valued real estate at death: his principal Braintree farm was the leased Tyng tenancy he never owned, the one freehold he had held outright (the Monatiquot house and orchard) he had sold to Richard Thayer in February 1661/2, and his sole land entry — the Quinapaug interest — was an unpriced frontier share the appraisers 'know not.' The £55 14s 6d therefore measures his movable estate alone.

row.short_label: Record coverage: a continuous 1641-1663 civic/land/court/probate footprint
row.statement: John Gurney's surviving documentary footprint is broad within four record classes — colony court and account records, town land books (Weymouth, Braintree, Billerica, Mendon), a registry deed, a court deposition, and probate (as witness/appraiser and as decedent) — and runs continuously from his earliest secure record (the 2 June 1641 Weymouth gunpowder-fine remission) to his 16 March 1663 estate inventory.

row.short_label: Anderson GMD p.158 - published coverage summary; origin 'Unknown'
row.statement: Anderson's Great Migration Directory (2nd ed., 2025), p. 158, summarizes John Gurney's documented New England presence — arrival 1636, settlements Boston and Braintree — records his English origin as 'Unknown,' and rests the entry on six cited records (Winthrop's Journal 2:422; Massachusetts Bay Records 1:331; NEHGR 62:94; Suffolk Probate Case #338; History of Weymouth 3:251; The American Genealogist 10:70-73); it omits the Weymouth residential phase the manuscript town-land records attest.

row.short_label: Analysis: the 1653 deposition is the only record of John's own person
row.statement: The 1653 Wilson v. Faxon deposition ('John Gurney of Brayntree aged 50 Yeares or thereabouts') is the only surviving record that attests a personal attribute of John Gurney himself; every other record fixes his property, credit, or a civic/probate office rather than his person. A man documented across four record classes over two decades is thus attested as a person, as opposed to as a landholder, creditor, or estate, by a single line in one court file. (The weight of the stated age and its birth inference are worked in the origin/age analysis, not here.)

row.short_label: Negative: no vital or church record fixes John's birth, marriage, death, or burial
row.statement: No New England vital or church record fixes John Gurney's own birth, first marriage (to Mary), death, or burial: within the surviving town vital records, church-admission records, and freeman lists naming John Gurney Sr. (c. 1636-1663), none preserves a baptism, marriage, death, or burial entry for him, and he appears on no church-admission or freeman roll — a silence Anderson's full-dress directory review reflects. His birth survives only as an inference from the 1653 deposition age and his death only as the terminus his March 1663 inventory implies. Scope limits: the one Braintree line matching his traditional 1661 remarriage and his second wife's 1661 death is printed under 'John Cheny'/'Grizell Kidbee' in the 1886 edition and is a distinct reading/identity question, counted here as neither a surviving nor an absent Gurney vital record; and absence in the reviewed set is not proof no such entry ever existed.

row.short_label: Negative: no record states John's English origin
row.statement: No record of John Gurney in New England states his English origin, parentage, or pre-migration residence; the colony, town, court, and probate records that document his American life are uniformly silent on where he came from, and Anderson's Great Migration Directory, having reviewed that surviving set, records the origin as 'Unknown.' This delimits the coverage of the record, not the identity question itself: the English-origin identification (Banks's Bury St Edmunds lead; the Candidate-B reading making John a son of Francis Gurney the Merchant Taylor) is an open matter pursued in the dedicated origin/identity work and is neither resolved nor advocated here.

row.short_label: Anderson GMD (2025): arrival 1636, Boston/Braintree, origin Unknown
row.statement: Robert Charles Anderson's Great Migration Directory (2nd ed., 2025), p. 158, records John Gurney with an arrival of 1636 and New England residences at Boston and Braintree (Weymouth not listed), while leaving his English origin 'Unknown' — the standing published assessment of John's arrival and settlement.

row.short_label: Absent from Weymouth's 1636 Fresh Pond great-lot roll
row.statement: John Gurney is absent from Weymouth's 1636 Fresh Pond 'great lot' roll of sixteen named householders - evidence he was not yet a Weymouth householder as early as 1636, consistent with an arrival after 1636 rather than with the town's founding cohort.

row.short_label: 1651-52 great lot = proprietary right, not residence (John Read comparator)
row.statement: John Gurney's 1651-52 Weymouth great lot no. 16 was part of a deferred laying-out of 'formerly granted' rights that demonstrably carried absentees and dead men (Samuel Newman and John Allin removed to Rehoboth, Thomas Rider to Boston, William Brandon dead by 1647), so his place on it reflects a surviving proprietary entitlement rather than residence; the closest comparator is John Read, who likewise held Weymouth land, took a Tyng Mount Wollaston farm, removed to Rehoboth, and still drew an 18-acre 1651-52 Fresh Pond great lot.

row.short_label: Grants sat inside an Aylesbury-Vale Bucks neighbour cluster (reception)
row.statement: John Gurney's East and Mill Field neighbours formed a coherent Aylesbury-Vale Buckinghamshire settler cluster - Robert Randall of Wendover, William Brandon of Ashton Clinton, and the Hunt/Humphrey families of Lee, whose Buckinghamshire origins are sworn in a 1688 Weymouth deposition (Massachusetts State Archives 129:16) - so his grants mark him as a newcomer received into an established, regionally-clustered Weymouth neighbourhood. The bearing of this cluster on John's own English origin is developed in the immigration-by-association topic, not here.
